newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korean rulers report rift with military.
newsitem.headline: North Korean rulers report rift with military.

text.p: North Korean rulers have revealed to a visiting U.S. Senate delegation that there is a rift with their own powerful military over holding peace talks before more international aid arrives in the famine-hit nation.

The issue, involving supply of 1.5 million tonnes of grain outside of immediate humanitarian food aid, has become the last hurdle to starting talks to formally close down the world's final Cold War frontier and officially end the 1950-53 Korean war.

Members of the delegation told a news conference in Tokyo on Saturday that top North Korean officials were surprisingly frank in warning military opposition could scuttle the talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.
Stalinist North Korea has been devastated by two years of floods, creating serious food shortages which aid agencies say places it just weeks away from disaster.

But the delegation said the sticking point was not immediate food supplies but military unhappiness that aid has not arrived which North Korea says was promised in a 1994 pact which persuaded Pyongyang to end a nuclear weapons programme.
"Our hosts in North Korea stressed their concerns that insufficient progress had been made in fulfilling the terms of the 1994 agreed framework," the senators said in a statement.

The senators met in Pyongyang on Friday with North Korean First Vice Foreign Minister Kang Sok-ju and Kim Kye Gwan, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee. Both men are regarded as close to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
However military officials snubbed the group of five, which was led by Ted Stevens (R-Alaska), chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, a key player in U.S. aid efforts.
The other senators, all members of the committee, were Daniel Inouye (D-Hawaii), Thad Cochran (R-Mississippi), Pete Domenici (R-New Mexico) and Pat Roberts (R-Kansas)

"We regret that we did not meet with officials of the Korean People's Army," the senators said in a statement. "Failure by the North Korean military to support and participate in the negotiations .... could pose an insurmountable obstacle."
There have regular reports of a power struggle involving the military, which analysts believe does not fully back apparent efforts by Kim Jong-il to end North Korea's isolation.

"I think that we were led to believe that there is a rift. The military is disturbed that the civilian authorities have not been able to obtain the food and fuel they'd been told they'd get," Stevens said.

"I don't know if that was just rattling the cage for us or whether it was stated as a fear, he said. "But it was a flat statement that they were worried about the reaction of their military if we were unable to assure them that they would receive the assistance they sought."
Domenici said the officials were open and forthright in saying "they were not sure how the military would respond to participation in the peace talks."
"It wasn't anything said secretly," Domenici said.

In Seoul on Saturday, U.S. Vice-President Al Gore also discussed ways to convince North Korea to join the talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam after a visit to China where he discussed the issue with Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
In agreeing to discuss possible peace talks, Pyongyang has insisted that as a pre-condition the United States and South Korea promise first to supply substantial food aid.
But the United States has firmly rejected pre-conditions while promising "good things will happen" once talks start.
Inouye, the delegation's only Democrat, said North Korean officials indicated once the issue of the 1.5 million tonnes was cleared up, a definite date could be set for the start of talks.
